html:
The main culture of central and western Europe in the late Bronze Age and early Iron Age, from about 1200 to 450 BCE. The map uses the label in 400 BCE for a huge area from Iberia to the Black Sea, as a broad sign for Iron Age Europe.

It is named after Hallstatt, a salt-mining village in the Austrian Alps, where a large cemetery was dug from 1846. Its salt made the area rich. The culture grew out of the Urnfield cultures, and in its later phase it spread iron tools and weapons across Europe.

In the 7th and 6th centuries BCE chiefs in eastern France and southern Germany lived in hillforts such as the Heuneburg and were buried in wagon graves with imported luxuries. The Vix grave in Burgundy held a woman with a huge Greek bronze krater, which came by trade through the Greek colony of Massalia. Around 450 BCE these princely centres declined and the La Tène culture took over. Both are linked with the early Celts.
